title: Philemon et Baucis
titleEn: A Thousand Doors, and One Open — Metamorphoses VIII.611–724
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Achelous falls silent, one of his hearers jeers that the gods cannot be so powerful, and old Lelex answers with a tale from the Phrygian hills: Jupiter and Mercury, walking in mortal shape, are shut out of a thousand houses and taken in by Baucis and Philemon in a reed-thatched cottage. The meal the two old people set out, the wine that refills itself unpoured, the drowning of the neighbourhood that shut its doors, and the end the couple ask for and are granted — one hour to take them both — carry the rest of the part.

sentences.t:
Amnis ab his tacuit. Factum mirabile cunctos
moverat:
sentences.l: After these things the river fell silent. A marvellous deed had moved them all:
sentences.i: With that the river fell silent. The marvel had moved them all —
sentences.n: “Amnis”, “the river”, is the speaker who has just finished, and “ab his”, literally “from these things”, means “after these words”. The pluperfect “moverat” puts the effect of the story in place before the reaction that follows in the present tense.

sentences.t:
inridet credentes, utque deorum
spretor erat mentisque ferox, Ixione natus
“ficta refers nimiumque putas Acheloe potentes
esse deos” dixit, “si dant adimuntque figuras.”
sentences.l: he laughs at those who believe; and, as he was a scorner of the gods and savage in mind, the one born of Ixion said, “You report made-up things, and you think the gods too powerful, Achelous, if they give shapes and take them away.”
sentences.i: he jeers at the ones who believe it; and, scorner of the gods that he was, and savage in temper, the son of Ixion said, “What you report is invented, Achelous, and you credit the gods with far too much power, if they hand out shapes and take them back.”
sentences.n: The present “inridet” cuts straight across the pluperfect “moverat” of the line before: the narrative drops into the historic present at the moment of the interruption. “Spretor”, an agent-noun built from “sperno”, “to spurn”, governs the genitive “deorum” — a professional despiser of gods — and “mentis” is a genitive of respect with “ferox”, fierce as to his mind. “Ixione natus”, “born of Ixion”, names the speaker by his father instead of by name, with the ablative of origin that is the standard idiom for descent. “Ficta” is the neuter plural participle of “fingo” used as a noun, “things moulded up”, and “nimium ... potentes esse deos” is an accusative-and-infinitive after “putas”, with “nimium” qualifying the adjective, not the verb.

sentences.t:
Obstipuere omnes nec talia dicta probarunt,
ante omnesque Lelex, animo maturus et aevo,
sic ait:
sentences.l: All were stunned, and did not approve such words, and before all of them Lelex, ripe in mind and in age, speaks thus:
sentences.i: They were all struck dumb, and no one approved of such talk, and Lelex before them all — a man ripe in mind and in years — says this:
sentences.n: “Obstipuere” is “obstipuerunt”: the poetic third-plural perfect in “-ere” runs all through this part — “clausere”, “consenuere”, “tetigere”, “voluere”, “fuere” — and always means exactly what the “-erunt” form means, while “probarunt” is the syncopated “probaverunt”. “Ante omnes”, “before all”, is “more than all the rest” rather than a statement of where he stood, and “animo ... et aevo” are ablatives of respect with “maturus”. “Ait” is a defective verb surviving in only a few forms, and the present here reports a past act.

sentences.t:
“Inmensa est finemque potentia caeli
non habet, et quidquid superi voluere, peractum est.
sentences.l: “The power of heaven is measureless and has no end, and whatever the gods above have willed has been carried through.
sentences.i: “The power of heaven is beyond measure and knows no limit; whatever the gods above have willed has been accomplished.
sentences.n: Magnus prints “Inmensa”, the unassimilated spelling of “immensa”, and keeps the same habit at “inmunibus” in 690 and “inlita” in 670. “Caeli”, “of heaven”, is the sky as the dwelling of the gods, so the power of heaven is the power of those who live there. “Voluere” is “voluerunt”.

sentences.t:
Quoque minus dubites, tiliae contermina quercus
collibus est Phrygiis modico circumdata muro.
sentences.l: And that you may doubt the less: on the Phrygian hills there is an oak bordering on a linden, ringed by a modest wall.
sentences.i: And so that you may doubt it the less — on the hills of Phrygia there stands an oak next to a linden, with a low wall running round the two of them.
sentences.n: “Quoque” here is not the adverb “also”: it is “quō-que”, “and in order that”, the purpose conjunction “quo” that regularly introduces a clause containing a comparative — “quo minus dubites”, “so that you may doubt less”. “Contermina”, “sharing a boundary”, takes the dative “tiliae”. These two trees are what the whole story exists to account for; they are still standing at 719–720.

sentences.t:
Ipse locum vidi; nam me Pelopeia Pittheus
misit in arva, suo quondam regnata parenti.
sentences.l: I myself saw the place; for Pittheus sent me into the fields of Pelops, once reigned over by his own father.
sentences.i: I saw the place myself; Pittheus sent me into the lands of Pelops, which his own father had once ruled.
sentences.n: Pittheus, king of Troezen, was a son of Pelops, so “Pelopeia arva” are his father’s territory. “Regnata” is the passive participle of “regno”, a verb otherwise intransitive: poets make it transitive so that a land can be “reigned over”, and “suo parenti” is the dative of the agent that goes with such a participle. The eyewitness claim is Lelex’s direct answer to the charge of making things up at 614.

sentences.t:
Haud procul hinc stagnum est, tellus habitabilis olim,
nunc celebres mergis fulicisque palustribus undae.
sentences.l: Not far from here there is a standing pool, land habitable once, now waters crowded with divers and marsh coots.
sentences.i: Not far from here there is a stagnant pool — habitable ground once, now water thronged with divers and marsh coots.
sentences.n: Two appositions do the work of a whole narrative: the same spot named as land “once” and as water “now”, with no verb in either phrase. “Celebres” with the ablative “mergis fulicisque” is “thronged with”, the adjective used of a crowded place. The pool is where the story ends up at 696–697.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter huc specie mortali cumque parente
venit Atlantiades positis caducifer alis.
sentences.l: Jupiter came here in mortal appearance, and with his father came the descendant of Atlas, the caduceus-bearer, with his wings laid aside.
sentences.i: Jupiter came to this place in mortal shape, and with his father came the son of Atlas’s line, bearer of the herald’s staff, with his wings laid aside.
sentences.n: “Atlantiades ... caducifer” is Mercury, descended from Atlas through his mother Maia and named from the staff he carries; “parente” is Jupiter, his father. “Positis ... alis”, “with his wings laid aside”, is an ablative absolute — a self-contained “with X done” phrase where English wants a clause — and you will meet several more of them in this part.

sentences.t:
Mille domos adiere locum requiemque petentes,
mille domos clausere serae.
sentences.l: They approached a thousand houses, seeking a place and rest; a thousand houses the door-bars closed.
sentences.i: They went up to a thousand houses, asking shelter and rest; a thousand houses had their bars shut against them.
sentences.n: The repeated “mille domos” at the head of both clauses sets the refusal against the request with no connecting word between them. In the second clause the subject is “serae”, the door-bars, which do the shutting themselves: the householders are never named or blamed here. “Adiere” and “clausere” are the “-ere” perfects.

sentences.t:
Tamen una recepit,
parva quidem, stipulis et canna tecta palustri;
sentences.l: One, however, received them — small indeed, roofed with straw and marsh reed;
sentences.i: One house, though, took them in — a small one, to be sure, thatched with straw and reed from the marsh;
sentences.n: “Una” is feminine because “domus” carries over from the line before, and “parva” and “tecta” agree with it. “Tecta” here is the participle of “tego”, “to cover”, with ablatives of material — not the noun “tecta”, “roofs”, which turns up at 691, 697 and 701.

sentences.t:
sed pia Baucis anus parilique aetate Philemon
illa sunt annis iuncti iuvenalibus, illa
consenuere casa paupertatemque fatendo
effecere levem nec iniqua mente ferendo.
sentences.l: but dutiful Baucis, an old woman, and Philemon of a like age were joined in that house in their youthful years; in that cottage they grew old together, and by confessing their poverty they made it light, and by bearing it with no unfair mind.
sentences.i: but in that house dutiful old Baucis and Philemon, as old as she, were married in their young years, and in that cottage they grew old together, and they made their poverty light by owning to it, and by bearing it with no resentful spirit.
sentences.n: Both instances of “illa” are ablatives agreeing with “casa”, which arrives only at the end — “in that house”, “in that cottage” — with no preposition, and the repetition is the whole point: one roof for the length of a marriage. “Iuncti sunt” of a couple is the ordinary Latin for being married, “parili aetate” is an ablative of description, and “consenuere” is “consenuerunt”. “Fatendo” and “ferendo” are ablatives of the gerund, the means by which the poverty was made light, and “nec iniqua mente” is litotes: not “fair-minded” but the denial of its opposite, which in Latin is the stronger way to say it.

sentences.t:
Nec refert, dominos illic famulosne requiras:
tota domus duo sunt, idem parentque iubentque.
sentences.l: Nor does it matter whether you look there for masters or for servants: the whole household is two people; the same two both obey and command.
sentences.i: It makes no difference whether you look there for masters or for servants: the whole household is two people, and the same two obey and give the orders.
sentences.n: “Refert” is impersonal, “it matters”, and governs a double indirect question, “dominos ... famulosne”, with the second alternative marked by the enclitic “-ne”; “requiras” is subjunctive because the question is reported. “Tota domus duo sunt” sets a plural verb against a singular subject because the sense is plural — the house is two people — and “idem” is the nominative plural.

sentences.t:
Ergo ubi caelicolae parvos tetigere penates
submissoque humiles intrarunt vertice postes,
sentences.l: So when the heaven-dwellers had reached the small household gods and entered the low doorposts with head lowered,
sentences.i: So when the sky-dwellers had reached those small household gods and had stooped their heads through the low doorway,
sentences.n: “Penates” are the household gods and, by metonymy, the house itself: gods of heaven arriving at the gods of a hut. “Submisso ... vertice”, “with head lowered”, is an ablative absolute, and the point of it is that the doorway is too low for them. “Intrarunt” is syncopated “intraverunt”, “tetigere” is “tetigerunt”.

sentences.t:
membra senex posito iussit relevare sedili,
quo superiniecit textum rude sedula Baucis.
sentences.l: the old man, a bench having been set out, bade them rest their limbs, and over that bench busy Baucis threw a rough woven thing.
sentences.i: the old man set out a bench and told them to rest their limbs, and over it painstaking Baucis threw a coarse woven cloth.
sentences.n: “Posito ... sedili” is an ablative absolute, “a seat having been set down”: the old man both provides the bench and issues the invitation. “Quo” is the ablative of the relative picking up “sedili”, “over which” — English has to name the seat again to keep the reference clear. “Textum rude” is a neuter participle used as a noun, “a rough woven thing”, and “sedula” is “busy, painstaking” — the word for someone who will not sit down.

sentences.t:
Inque foco tepidum cinerem dimovit et ignes
suscitat hesternos foliisque et cortice sicco
nutrit et ad flammas anima producit anili.
sentences.l: And on the hearth she pushed aside the warm ash and rouses yesterday’s fires, and with leaves and dry bark she feeds them, and brings them out to flames with an old woman’s breath.
sentences.i: And on the hearth she pushed the warm ash apart and wakes yesterday’s embers, feeds them with leaves and dry bark, and with an old woman’s breath brings them up into flame.
sentences.n: The tense changes inside a single sentence: “dimovit” is perfect, “suscitat”, “nutrit” and “producit” present — Ovid alternates the two all through this scene, the present pulling the reader into the action as it is happening, and the sense of the story does not change with it. “Ignes hesternos”, “yesterday’s fires”, are embers still alive from the night before, and “anima ... anili”, “with an aged woman’s breath”, is an ablative of means: she blows on them, and the adjective keeps her age in view while she works. “Producit ad flammas” is “leads forward as far as flames”, the fire drawn out until it blazes.

sentences.t:
Multifidasque faces ramaliaque arida tecto
detulit et minuit parvoque admovit aeno.
sentences.l: And she brought down from the roof many-cleft torch-wood and dry twigs, and made them small, and moved them up to a small bronze pot.
sentences.i: And she brought split kindling and dry twigs down from the roof, chopped them small, and pushed them under a little bronze pot.
sentences.n: “Tecto” is the ablative of the place from which, “from the roof”: the dry wood is stored up under the thatch. “Multifidas faces” is torch-wood split into many strips. Three perfects in a row, “detulit ... minuit ... admovit”, bring the narrative back to past time after the presents of the two lines before, and “aeno” is the dative after “admovit”.

sentences.t:
Quodque suus coniunx riguo conlegerat horto,
truncat holus foliis;
sentences.l: And the greenstuff which her own husband had gathered in the watered garden, she docks of its leaves;
sentences.i: And the greens her own husband had gathered in the well-watered garden she strips of their leaves;
sentences.n: The antecedent stands inside its own relative clause — “quod ... holus”, “which vegetable” — so “holus” is at once the object of “conlegerat” and the object of “truncat”. “Truncat holus foliis” is “docks the vegetable of its leaves”, with an ablative of separation. “Suus” refers back to the subject of the main verb, so the husband is hers: Baucis is still the one working.

sentences.t:
furca levat illa bicorni
sordida terga suis nigro pendentia tigno
servatoque diu resecat de tergore partem
exiguam sectamque domat ferventibus undis.
sentences.l: with a two-horned fork she lifts down the grimy chine of a pig, hanging from a black beam, and from the long-kept chine she cuts off a scanty part, and the cut piece she tames in boiling water.
sentences.i: with a two-pronged fork she lifts down a grimy side of pork that hangs from a blackened beam, and from the long-hoarded chine she cuts a meagre portion, and tames the slice in boiling water.
sentences.n: “Terga suis”, literally “the backs of a pig”, is a poetic plural for the one smoked chine; it hangs in the smoke of the hearth, which is why it is “sordida”, filthy, and the beam “nigro”, blackened. “Servato diu ... tergore” is the ablative after “de”: the one piece of meat in the house has been hoarded, not eaten, the portion cut is “exiguam”, scanty, and “domat”, “tames, breaks in”, is the word for boiling meat soft — the metaphor is Ovid’s and both layers keep it. Magnus prints “illa”, so it is Baucis who reaches the meat down; some editions print “ille”, which makes it Philemon.

sentences.t: Interea medias fallunt sermonibus horas
sentences.l: Meanwhile they cheat the hours in between with talk
sentences.i: Meanwhile they beguile the intervening hours with conversation
sentences.n: “Fallere horas”, “to cheat the hours”, is the idiom for passing time so that it is not felt, and “medias” is the time in the middle, between the arrival and the meal. The line numbering jumps from 651 to 655 because Magnus deletes 652–654 as not Ovid’s and prints them nowhere: nothing has dropped out of the text.

sentences.t:
concutiuntque torum de molli fluminis ulva
impositum lecto sponda pedibusque salignis.
sentences.l: and they shake up a mattress of soft river sedge, laid on a couch with willow frame and feet.
sentences.i: and they plump up a mattress of soft river sedge, laid on a couch whose frame and legs were willow.
sentences.n: “De molli fluminis ulva”, “out of the river’s soft sedge”, gives what the mattress is stuffed with; “impositum” agrees with “torum” and sets it on the couch. “Sponda pedibusque salignis” is an ablative of description attached to “lecto”: frame and feet both of willow, and the willow comes back at 659.

sentences.t:
Vestibus hunc velant, quas non nisi tempore festo
sternere consuerant: sed et haec vilisque vetusque
vestis erat, lecto non indignanda saligno.
sentences.l: They veil it with cloths which they were accustomed to spread only at festival time: but this cloth too was both cheap and old, not to be disdained by a willow couch.
sentences.i: They cover it with cloths they used to spread only on a feast day: but this cloth too was cheap and old — nothing a willow couch could think beneath it.
sentences.n: “Hunc” is the mattress of 655, “non nisi”, “not except”, is the ordinary Latin way of saying “only”, and “consuerant” is syncopated “consueverant”. “Indignanda” is a gerundive of the deponent “indignor”, “to think unworthy”: the verb is active in meaning but its gerundive is passive in force, which is why the literal reads “not to be disdained”. “Lecto ... saligno” is the dative of the agent that regularly accompanies a gerundive — the couch is the one who would do the disdaining — and the joke is that the furniture is exactly as poor as the cloth.

sentences.t:
Accubuere dei. Mensam succincta tremensque
ponit anus,
sentences.l: The gods reclined. The old woman, girt up and trembling, sets a table,
sentences.i: The gods took their places at the couch. The old woman, skirts hitched up and shaking, sets out a table,
sentences.n: “Accubuere” is “accubuerunt”; to “lie down beside” is the posture of a Roman dinner, so the two gods dine as ordinary guests. “Succincta”, “girt up”, is used of clothing tucked out of the way for work, and “tremens” is the shaking of age — at this point in the story she has no idea who her guests are.

sentences.t:
mensae sed erat pes tertius impar.
Testa parem fecit.
sentences.l: but to the table there was a third foot unequal. A potsherd made it equal.
sentences.i: but the table had a third leg that was short. A potsherd made it even.
sentences.n: “Mensae erat pes”, “there was a leg to the table”, is the dative of possession, the standard Latin way of saying whose a thing is; English inverts it into “the table had”. “Impar” and “parem” state the fault and its remedy with the same adjective, negative and then positive, in successive lines.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam subdita clivum
sustulit, aequatam mentae tersere virentes.
sentences.l: And when this, put underneath, had taken away the slope, green mint-sprigs wiped the levelled table.
sentences.i: And once the sherd, wedged underneath, had taken out the tilt, green mint wiped the table, now level.
sentences.n: “Quae” opens the sentence as a connecting relative reaching back to “testa”, the potsherd — “and when this ...” — which is what Latin does where English would start a new sentence with “it”. “Clivum sustulit” is literally “lifted away the slope”, and “aequatam” agrees with the table understood. “Tersere” is “terserunt”; mint is rubbed over the wood both to clean it and to scent it.

sentences.t:
Ponitur hic bicolor sincerae baca Minervae
conditaque in liquida corna autumnalia faece
sentences.l: Here is set the two-coloured berry of unsullied Minerva, and autumn cornel-cherries stored in liquid lees,
sentences.i: On it are set the two-coloured berry of chaste Minerva, autumn cornel-cherries put up in runny wine-lees,
sentences.n: “Baca Minervae”, “Minerva’s berry”, is the olive, the goddess’s own gift, and “bicolor” because green and black olives are served together; “sincerae”, “unmixed, untainted”, belongs to the virgin goddess. The singular “ponitur” heads a list of several dishes, agreeing with the first item only and doing duty for all of them.

sentences.t:
intibaque et radix et lactis massa coacti
ovaque non acri leviter versata favilla,
omnia fictilibus.
sentences.l: and endives and radish and a lump of curdled milk and eggs lightly turned in ash that was not fierce — all in earthenware.
sentences.i: endives and radish, a lump of curdled milk, and eggs lightly turned in ash that was not too hot — everything of it in earthenware.
sentences.n: “Lactis massa coacti” is cheese described by how it is made: milk “driven together”, curdled. “Non acri ... favilla” is an ablative of place — the eggs are turned in warm ash at the edge of the fire, not in the flame. “Omnia fictilibus” has no verb at all, and the bare ablative “fictilibus”, “in clay ware”, delivers the household’s poverty in two words.

sentences.t:
Post haec caelatus eodem
sistitur argento crater fabricataque fago
pocula, qua cava sunt, flaventibus inlita ceris.
sentences.l: After these things a mixing-bowl chased in the same silver is set up, and cups made out of beech, smeared, where they are hollow, with yellow waxes.
sentences.i: After this a mixing-bowl, embossed in the same silver, is set out, and cups made of beechwood, coated with yellow wax where they are hollowed out.
sentences.n: The joke is in “eodem argento”, “the same silver”: everything just listed was in earthenware, so “the same silver” is clay, and “caelatus”, the technical word for chased or embossed metalwork, is used with a straight face of a clay bowl. A “crater” is the bowl in which wine is mixed with water before it is poured. “Fago” is the ablative of material, and “qua cava sunt”, “in the part where they are hollow”, means on the inside: the wax seals the wood so the cups will hold wine, and “inlita” is Magnus’s unassimilated spelling of “illita”.

sentences.t: Parva mora est, epulasque foci misere calentes,
sentences.l: There is a small delay, and the hearths sent out steaming dishes,
sentences.i: A short wait, and the hearth sent up the dishes, steaming,
sentences.n: “Parva mora est” stands in the present for the pause itself, and then “misere” — “miserunt” — drops back into the perfect. “Foci”, “hearths”, is a poetic plural for the one fire, and it is the hearth, not the cook, that is made the subject of the sending.

sentences.t:
nec longae rursus referuntur vina senectae
dantque locum mensis paulum seducta secundis.
sentences.l: and wines of no long old age are carried back again, and, drawn a little aside, they give place to the second courses.
sentences.i: and the wine, of no great age, is carried back again and drawn a little aside, giving room to the second course.
sentences.n: “Longae ... senectae” is a genitive of quality with “vina”: wine that has no long old age to it, that is, young and cheap. “Mensae secundae”, “the second tables”, is the Roman name for the dessert course. “Seducta” is neuter plural agreeing with “vina” — the wine is shifted aside, not taken away.

sentences.t:
Hic nux, hic mixta est rugosis carica palmis
prunaque et in patulis redolentia mala canistris
et de purpureis conlectae vitibus uvae.
sentences.l: Here is a nut, here a Carian fig mixed with wrinkled dates, and plums, and, in wide baskets, sweet-smelling apples, and grapes gathered from purple vines.
sentences.i: Here a nut, here a fig out of Caria mixed among shrivelled dates, and plums, and fragrant apples in broad baskets, and grapes gathered off purple vines.
sentences.n: “Carica” is a dried fig named from Caria, the region that exported them — the fruit identified by where it came from, as the olive at 664 was identified by its goddess — and “mixta est” is singular because it agrees with “carica” alone. “In patulis ... canistris” is split apart around the words it belongs with, the ordinary poetic interlocking that lets the baskets frame their own contents, and “de purpureis vitibus” is an ablative of source with “conlectae”, the vine called purple for the fruit it carries.

sentences.t:
Candidus in medio favus est. Super omnia vultus
accessere boni nec iners pauperque voluntas.
sentences.l: In the middle is a gleaming honeycomb. Above all these, kindly faces were added, and a willingness neither idle nor poor.
sentences.i: In the middle of it all, a honeycomb, shining white. And on top of it all came kindly faces, and a goodwill that was neither idle nor poor.
sentences.n: “Candidus” is bright, gleaming white, not merely “white”: after a catalogue of dark and wrinkled fruit, the comb is the one shining thing on the table, and five words make a complete sentence that closes the list. “Super omnia” then works both ways at once, on top of everything laid out and above everything in worth, and “accessere” is “accesserunt”, “came in addition”. “Nec iners pauperque” is litotes again, and it is pointed: the poverty that is a plain fact of the house is denied of the spirit that serves the meal.

sentences.t:
Interea totiens haustum cratera repleri
sponte sua per seque vident succrescere vina:
sentences.l: Meanwhile they see the mixing-bowl, drained so often, being refilled, and the wines growing up again of their own accord and by themselves:
sentences.i: Meanwhile they see the bowl they had drained so many times filling again, and the wine rising back of its own accord, all by itself:
sentences.n: “Cratera” keeps the Greek accusative ending of the loan-word “crater”; it is the subject-accusative of the infinitive “repleri”, not an accusative of respect. Two accusative-and-infinitive clauses hang from “vident”: the bowl to be refilled, and the wine to grow back. “Sponte sua per seque” doubles the idea — by its own will and through itself — because the whole miracle is that nobody is pouring.

sentences.t:
attoniti novitate pavent manibusque supinis
concipiunt Baucisque preces timidusque Philemon
et veniam dapibus nullisque paratibus orant.
sentences.l: thunderstruck at the strangeness they take fright, and with upturned hands both Baucis and frightened Philemon frame prayers, and they beg pardon for the banquet and for their non-existent preparations.
sentences.i: struck senseless by the strangeness, they take fright, and with palms turned upward Baucis and frightened Philemon put together a prayer, and beg pardon for the meal, and for having made no preparation at all.
sentences.n: “Manibus supinis”, “with hands laid back”, is the Roman posture of prayer, palms turned up to the sky, and “concipere preces” is the technical phrase for reciting a prayer in its set form of words, not for improvising one; the two names arrive only after two plural verbs have been waiting for them. “Veniam orant” with the datives “dapibus ... paratibus” asks forgiveness for the things named, and “nullis paratibus”, literally “no preparations”, is the sharper Latin idiom: the negative is attached to the noun rather than standing as a separate word, so what they apologise for is a nothing.

sentences.t:
Unicus anser erat, minimae custodia villae:
quem dis hospitibus domini mactare parabant.
sentences.l: There was a single goose, the guardianship of the tiniest of farmsteads; and it the masters were preparing to slaughter for their divine guests.
sentences.i: They had one goose, the whole watch of that smallest of farmsteads; and the masters were getting ready to kill it for their divine guests.
sentences.n: “Custodia”, an abstract noun meaning “guard-duty”, stands for the concrete guard: the goose is the farm’s watchman. The same figure returns at 711, where the couple themselves are the temple’s “tutela”. “Quem” is a connecting relative opening the second clause, “and it”, and “dis hospitibus” is a dative — the guests are gods, and the bird is for them.

sentences.t:
Ille celer penna tardos aetate fatigat
eluditque diu tandemque est visus ad ipsos
confugisse deos.
sentences.l: It, swift in wing, wears out the two who are slow with age, and eludes them a long while, and at last seemed to have fled for refuge to the gods themselves.
sentences.i: The bird, quick on the wing, wears the two of them out, slow as they are with age, dodges them a long while, and at last seemed to have taken refuge with the gods themselves.
sentences.n: “Celer penna” and “tardos aetate” are matched ablatives of respect — fast as to wing against slow as to age — and “tardos” is the accusative object of “fatigat”, the old pair. “Visus est confugisse”, “was seen to have fled”, in this idiom comes close to “appeared to”, and Ovid leaves it open whether the goose sought the gods out or only seemed to.

sentences.l: The gods above forbade it to be killed. “And we are gods,” they said, “and the godless neighbourhood will pay the penalties it has deserved”;
sentences.i: The gods above forbade the killing. “And we are gods,” they said, “and this godless neighbourhood will pay the penalty it has earned”;
sentences.n: “Vetuere necari” puts a passive infinitive after “veto” with no subject expressed, “forbade that it be killed”. The enclitic “-que” is printed outside the quotation marks, “di” que, because it joins this sentence to the last while grammatically belonging to the word inside. “Vicinia”, “the neighbourhood”, is the abstract standing for the people in it, and “impia” is the charge against them: they failed the duty owed to a guest.

sentences.t:
“vobis inmunibus huius
esse mali dabitur.
sentences.l: “to you it will be granted to be free of this evil.
sentences.i: “It will be granted to you to go untouched by this ruin.
sentences.n: “Dabitur” is impersonal, “it will be given”, with the infinitive “esse” as its subject and the dative “vobis” as the one it is given to; “inmunibus” is predicative and agrees with that dative. “Immunis”, “exempt”, takes the genitive of what one is exempt from, here “huius mali”. Magnus’s “inmunibus” is his unassimilated spelling again.

sentences.t:
Modo vestra relinquite tecta
ac nostros comitate gradus et in ardua montis
ite simul.”
sentences.l: Only leave your dwellings, and accompany our steps, and go together into the steep parts of the mountain.”
sentences.i: Only leave your house, come along with us, and climb the steep of the mountain together.”
sentences.n: “Comitate” is an imperative of the active “comito”; the verb is normally deponent, “comitor”, which would give “comitamini”, and the older active form survives in verse. “In ardua montis” is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun with a partitive genitive, “into the steep places of the mountain”. “Modo”, “only, just”, takes some of the edge off a command.

sentences.t:
Parent ambo baculisque levati
nituntur longo vestigia ponere clivo.
sentences.l: Both obey, and, lifted by their sticks, they strive to set their footprints on the long slope.
sentences.i: The two of them obey, and, propped on their sticks, they labour to plant their steps up the long slope.
sentences.n: “Baculis levati”, “lifted by staffs”, is an ablative of means with a passive participle: the sticks take their weight. “Nituntur” is deponent — passive in form, active in meaning, “they strain” — and “vestigia ponere”, “to set footprints”, is the ordinary phrase for walking, made heavy here by the effort it costs them.

sentences.t:
Tantum aberant summo, quantum semel ire sagitta
missa potest:
sentences.l: They were as far from the top as an arrow, once shot, is able to travel:
sentences.i: They were as far from the summit as an arrow can travel in a single flight:
sentences.n: “Tantum ... quantum” is the correlative pair, “so much ... as much as”, here measuring a distance. “Summo” is an ablative of separation with “aberant”, “were away from the top”. “Semel ire”, “to go once”, makes one flight of an arrow into a unit of measurement.

sentences.t:
flexere oculos et mersa palude
cetera prospiciunt, tantum sua tecta manere.
sentences.l: they turned their eyes and see that all the rest is sunk in the marsh, that only their own dwelling remains.
sentences.i: they turned to look, and see everything else sunk in the marsh, and only their own house still standing.
sentences.n: “Prospiciunt” governs two accusative-and-infinitive clauses with “esse” left out: “cetera mersa (esse)”, that all the rest is drowned, and “sua tecta manere”, that their own roof remains. The perfect “flexere” and the present “prospiciunt” sit in the same sentence — the turn is done, the seeing is still going on. This is the pool Lelex pointed to at 624–625.

sentences.t:
Dumque ea mirantur, dum deflent fata suorum,
illa vetus, dominis etiam casa parva duobus
vertitur in templum:
sentences.l: And while they wonder at these things, while they weep for the fates of their own people, that old cottage, small even for two owners, is turned into a temple:
sentences.i: And while they are still marvelling at it, still weeping for the fate of their own people, the old cottage, small even for two owners, turns into a temple:
sentences.n: “Dum” with a present indicative is “while”, and the present stays even where the narrative around it is past. “Suorum”, “their own people”, are the drowned neighbours, and the couple weep for the very neighbourhood the gods condemned at 689–690. “Dominis ... duobus” is a dative, “small even for two owners”, and the phrase reaches back to 636, where the whole household was two people.

sentences.t:
furcas subiere columnae,
stramina flavescunt, aurataque tecta videntur
caelataeque fores adopertaque marmore tellus.
sentences.l: columns went in under the forked props; the thatch turns yellow, and gilded roofs are seen, and chased doors, and ground covered over with marble.
sentences.i: columns came up under the forked props; the straw turns golden, and a gilded roof appears, and chased doors, and ground overlaid with marble.
sentences.n: “Subiere”, “subierunt”, is “went underneath”: the columns take the place of the forked poles by rising in under them, so the change is described as a movement rather than a substitution, and “flavescunt” is inchoative, “begin to turn yellow”, the present holding the straw in mid-change while they watch. One verb, “videntur”, then serves all three subjects that follow. “Caelatae fores” answers the “caelatus ... crater” of 668–669 — the chasing that was a joke on a clay bowl is now literally true — and “adoperta marmore” is an ablative of means.

sentences.t: Talia tum placido Saturnius edidit ore:
sentences.l: Then the son of Saturn uttered such words from a calm mouth:
sentences.i: Then the son of Saturn spoke out, and his mouth was calm:
sentences.n: “Saturnius”, “the Saturnian”, is Jupiter named from his father Saturn, exactly as the scoffer was named “Ixione natus” at 613. “Edidit ore”, “put forth from his mouth”, uses the ablative of source, and “placido” carries the tone: the god who has just drowned a district speaks gently.

sentences.t:
“Dicite, iuste senex et femina coniuge iusto
digna, quid optetis.”
sentences.l: “Say, just old man, and woman worthy of a just husband, what you two wish for.”
sentences.i: “Tell me, upright old man, and woman worthy of an upright husband, what you would ask for.”
sentences.n: “Iuste senex” and “femina ... digna” are vocatives, and “digna” takes the ablative “coniuge iusto”, worthy of the husband she has. “Quid optetis” is an indirect question after “dicite”, which is why the verb is subjunctive; it is plural, so the wish is to be theirs jointly.

sentences.t:
Cum Baucide pauca locutus
iudicium superis aperit commune Philemon:
sentences.l: Having spoken a few words with Baucis, Philemon opens their shared decision to the gods above:
sentences.i: After a few words with Baucis, Philemon lays their joint decision before the gods above:
sentences.n: “Locutus” is the perfect participle of the deponent “loquor”: passive in form, active in sense, “having spoken”. “Baucide” is the ordinary Latin ablative of a Greek-stem name (Baucis, Baucid-), whereas “Baucida” at 715 keeps the true Greek accusative ending “-a” where Latin would give “-em”. “Iudicium commune”, “the shared verdict”, is settled between them before it is spoken, and only one of them reports it.

sentences.t:
“Esse sacerdotes delubraque vestra tueri
poscimus;
sentences.l: “We ask to be priests and to guard your shrines;
sentences.i: “We ask to be your priests and to keep your shrines;
sentences.n: “Poscimus” is a firm verb — “we ask for”, close to “we claim” — but it is a request, and it governs two infinitives, “esse” and “tueri”; “sacerdotes” is nominative because the subject of the infinitive is the subject of “poscimus”. “Tueri” is deponent, active in meaning, “to watch over”. What they request is service, from a god who has just gilded a roof for them.

sentences.t:
et quoniam concordes egimus annos,
auferat hora duos eadem, ne coniugis umquam
busta meae videam neu sim tumulandus ab illa.”
sentences.l: and since we have passed our years of one mind, let one and the same hour carry off the two of us, so that I may never look on the pyre of my wife, nor be one who must be buried by her.”
sentences.i: and since we have lived out our years of one mind, let the same hour carry the two of us away, so that I may never look on my wife’s pyre, nor be the one she must bury.”
sentences.n: “Concordes” is predicative with “egimus annos”: not “harmonious years” but “we passed our years being in agreement”. “Auferat” is a jussive subjunctive, a wish put in the form of a command, and “eadem” is held back from “hora” so that “duos”, the two of them, stands between the hour and its sameness. “Ne ... neu”, “so that not ... and so that not”, is a negative purpose clause and its continuation, and “sim tumulandus” is the gerundive with “sum”, the construction of necessity, whose agent “ab illa” takes the preposition rather than the plain dative. Magnus prints “ne”, making this a purpose clause depending on the wish; some editions print “nec”, which turns it into a second wish set beside “auferat”.

sentences.t:
Vota fides sequitur. Templi tutela fuere,
donec vita data est.
sentences.l: Performance follows the prayers. They were the guardianship of the temple, as long as life was granted.
sentences.i: What they asked for was made good. They were the temple’s watch as long as life was granted them.
sentences.n: “Fides” here is the keeping of a pledge, so “fides sequitur vota” is “the making-good comes after the asking”. “Tutela”, an abstract noun used for the concrete guardians, matches “custodia” used of the goose at 684 — the two of them are now what the goose was to the farm. “Fuere” is “fuerunt”.

sentences.t:
Annis aevoque soluti
ante gradus sacros cum starent forte locique
narrarent casus,
sentences.l: Undone by years and by length of days, when they chanced to be standing before the sacred steps and were telling the fortunes of the place,
sentences.i: Undone by years and length of days, as they chanced to be standing before the sacred steps and telling the history of the place,
sentences.n: “Soluti”, “loosened, come apart”, is what age does to a body in Latin, with “annis aevoque” as ablatives of cause. “Cum ... starent ... narrarent” is circumstantial “cum” with the subjunctive, setting the scene for the main verb that arrives at 715. The pair have become the tellers of the story we are being told.

sentences.t:
frondere Philemona Baucis,
Baucida conspexit senior frondere Philemon
sentences.l: Baucis saw Philemon putting out leaves, and aged Philemon saw Baucis putting out leaves
sentences.i: Baucis saw Philemon coming into leaf, and old Philemon saw Baucis coming into leaf
sentences.n: “Philemona” and “Baucida” keep their Greek accusative endings. The word order mirrors itself across the line-break — “frondere Philemona Baucis” against “Baucida ... frondere Philemon”, the two names changing places as object and as subject — and the one verb “conspexit” serves both halves, so that each sees the other in the same instant. The archived text prints no stop after “Philemon” although the next line opens with a capital and the sense needs a full stop there; the text is left exactly as archived and the point is recorded.

sentences.t:
Iamque super geminos crescente cacumine vultus
mutua, dum licuit reddebant dicta
sentences.l: And now, with the tree-top growing over their twin faces, they were giving each other words in return, while it was allowed,
sentences.i: And now, as the tree-top rose over their two faces, they gave each other words back and forth while they still could,
sentences.n: “Crescente cacumine” is an ablative absolute, “with the tree-top growing”: it is what is happening while they are still speaking. “Mutua ... dicta”, “words given in return”, stand at the two ends of 717 with the whole clause “dum licuit reddebant” dropped in between. “Dum licuit”, “while it was permitted”, is impersonal, and what is closing the permission is the leaves.

sentences.t:
“vale” que
“o coniunx” dixere simul, simul abdita texit
ora frutex.
sentences.l: and “farewell” and “o my spouse” they said at one moment; at that same moment the shrub covered their faces and hid them.
sentences.i: and “farewell” — “o my spouse” — they said at the same moment, and at that same moment the foliage closed over their faces and hid them.
sentences.n: “Coniunx” serves for husband and for wife alike, so each says the identical word to the other and the two voices cannot be told apart. “Abdita ... ora” is proleptic: the participle states what the covering brings about, faces hidden by being covered. The repeated “simul ... simul” makes the farewell and the silencing a single event, and “dixere” is “dixerunt”.

sentences.t:
Ostendit adhuc Thyneius illic
incola de gemino vicinos corpore truncos.
sentences.l: The Thynian dweller there still points out the neighbouring trunks that came from the twin body.
sentences.i: The Thynian who lives there still points them out — trunks standing side by side, grown out of that twin body.
sentences.n: “Adhuc”, “to this day”, moves the story up to the moment of telling: the trees can be visited. “Thyneius incola” is the local inhabitant, Thynian, of Thynia in Bithynia, although the hills were called Phrygian at 621 — the geography here is loose. “Vicinos”, “neighbouring”, is the adjective belonging to “vicinia”, the neighbourhood condemned at 689–690: the only good neighbours left are the two trees.

sentences.t:
Haec mihi non vani (neque erat cur fallere vellent)
narravere senes:
sentences.l: These things old men told me, men not given to falsehood (nor was there any reason why they should want to deceive):
sentences.i: Old men told me all this — men not given to lying, and with no reason to want to deceive me:
sentences.n: “Non vani”, “not empty, not given to falsehood”, is litotes: the denial does the work of an adjective. “Erat cur ... vellent” is a relative clause with the subjunctive after a statement of existence, “there was a reason why they should wish”, and the whole parenthesis answers the charge of invented stories at 614. “Narravere” is “narraverunt”.

sentences.t:
equidem pendentia vidi
serta super ramos, ponensque recentia dixi
sentences.l: I for my part saw garlands hanging over the branches, and, laying fresh ones there, I said:
sentences.i: I saw the garlands hanging over the branches myself, and as I laid fresh ones there I said:
sentences.n: “Equidem” is emphatic with a first-person verb, “I for my part”: Lelex separates what he saw with his own eyes from what he was told. Garlands hung on a tree are a cult offering, so by adding new ones he makes himself a worshipper of the transformed pair. “Pendentia ... serta” is split around “vidi”.

sentences.t: “cura deum di sint, et qui coluere colantur.””
sentences.l: “Let those who are the gods’ care be gods, and let those who worshipped be worshipped.”
sentences.i: “Let those the gods care for be gods, and let those who gave worship receive it.”
sentences.n: “Deum” is the shortened genitive plural for “deorum”, common in verse, so “cura deum” is “the concern of the gods”. “Sint” and “colantur” are jussive subjunctives, a wish in two matched halves. “Coluere” is “coluerunt”, and the verb “colo” carries both senses at once, to tend and to worship, so the second half turns the first one inside out.
